content: 1. A clear distinction was made between two types of assessments: (i) the evaluation of the strength of evidence supporting causal inference, and (ii) the evaluation of confidence in the estimated effect sizes. This approach was adopted because evidence may support causation, indicating that reducing household air pollution (HAP) exposure would lead to health benefits, such as risk reduction. 2. The Hill viewpoints were applied to assess the strength of evidence for causal inference, while the GEPHI methodology, a revised version of GRADE, was used to evaluate confidence in effect sizes. It was acknowledged that some aspects of the evidence could be evaluated using both methods. 3. This dual approach—distinguishing causal inference from confidence in effect sizes—was primarily used to estimate the impacts of interventions on specific health outcomes. 4. Modifications to the GRADE methodology, referred to as GEPHI in this project, included the following: Non-randomized experimental evidence was categorized as moderate quality, though uncontrolled before-and-after studies were more likely to be downgraded. Evidence could be upgraded by one level if: 1. Studies with different designs and conducted in diverse settings reported similar effect directions, provided statistical heterogeneity was not significant. 2. Supportive analogous evidence was available from other combustion sources, such as ambient air pollution (AAP), second-hand smoke, or active smoking. The coherence of evidence contributing to different parts of the causal chain was assessed. 5. GEPHI assessment tables for two evidence reviews—impacts of interventions on health outcomes and impacts on kitchen HAP—were presented in a tabular format in Annex 5. These tables allowed for comparisons between standard GRADE and GEPHI assessments. 6. Non-randomized experimental studies were considered to provide stronger evidence for these guidelines because they offered insights into the effects of improved stoves and cleaner fuels on household air pollution and personal exposure levels. These studies were divided into two main groups: Cross-sectional or other designs comparing homes that voluntarily adopted cleaner fuels/technologies with those using traditional methods. Experimental designs where new fuels/technologies were introduced as part of a project or study, allowing for comparisons within the same home (as its own control) or with parallel control groups. 7. The first study design was deemed weaker due to the strong association between adopting improved fuels/technologies and socioeconomic or developmental factors, which could influence how the new technology was used. These factors were only partially controlled for in such studies. 8. The second study design was considered stronger because it controlled for these factors by using the home as its own control. However, variables such as seasonal practices and family size could still change over time. High-quality experimental studies recorded and controlled for these factors. 9. Non-randomized experimental studies that failed to address these issues and were subject to bias were downgraded in the GEPHI assessment. 10. Consistency of effect across different settings and study designs was used as a rationale for upgrading evidence. This approach drew on the Hill viewpoints, emphasizing the importance of obtaining similar results across diverse situations and techniques. 11. The strength of recommendations was determined using decision tables that considered the quality of evidence, certainty about harms and benefits, values and preferences, feasibility, and resource implications. Recommendations were categorized as: Strong: High certainty about evidence quality and feasibility, indicating implementation in most circumstances. Conditional: Less certainty about evidence quality and feasibility, meaning applicability may vary by context. 12. All decisions were reached by consensus during meetings or through the WHO-hosted EZCollab web platform. If disagreements arose, a two-thirds majority vote was required to finalize decisions. 13. The WHO Steering Group (SG) was involved in all stages of planning, evidence review, drafting recommendations, and consultations. Details of SG members are provided in Annex 1. 14. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) included experts in all relevant areas, with consideration for gender balance and regional diversity. Members defined key questions, conducted systematic reviews, drafted recommendations, and responded to external peer review comments. Their roles and expertise are detailed in Annex 1. 15. External peer reviewers (EPRG) were selected from subject experts, implementing agencies, and partners. They evaluated evidence reviews and final recommendations, with their comments informing revisions. Reviewer details are provided in Annex 1. 16. All GDG and EPRG members completed WHO declaration of interest forms, which were reviewed for potential conflicts. No conflicts required exclusion of any member from their role. 17. The recommendations focused on reducing emission rates and replacing specific fuels (e.g., coal, kerosene) due to their associated health and safety risks. Improved ventilation and behavioral changes were also recognized as important but secondary to reducing emissions. 18. Household energy interventions should consider multiple energy needs (e.g., cooking, heating, lighting) to avoid unintended consequences, such as reverting to traditional methods for warmth or light. 19. Policies promoting cleaner household combustion devices and fuels must ensure affordability and availability to prevent energy poverty and associated harms. 20. A systematic approach to monitoring and evaluation (M&E) is critical to track progress and provide feedback to stakeholders. 21. Safety concerns, such as risks of burns and house fires, must be addressed during the design, testing, and evaluation of new technologies and fuels to minimize injury risks.
